en: Angry and bitter in speech or debate
hook: ACRIMONIOUS: ACRID, as bitter as acid.
story: Acrimonious. Angry and bitter in speech or debate. At a residents' meeting in a city apartment building, the question was simple: who would pay to fix the broken lift? Within ten minutes, neighbours who had shared holiday sweets for years were shouting across the room, pointing fingers and dragging up old complaints about parking. Little Isla watched from the stairs, shocked at how acrimonious grown-ups could be. The acrimonious meeting ended with slammed doors. Acrimonious shares its root with acrid, meaning sharp and bitter, like burning smoke. So, what word describes a debate full of bitter, angry words? ... Acrimonious.

gre.s: What began as a friendly disagreement between the two scholars grew increasingly ____, until each was publicly accusing the other of fraud.
gre.clue: publicly accusing the other of fraud

example: The acrimonious split between the band's two founders played out for months in newspaper interviews and courtrooms.

en: Sharply severe or critical; also, causing skin tissue to contract
hook: ASTRINGENT: like a STRINGENT, tight squeeze, harsh.
story: Astringent. Sharply severe or critical; also, making skin tissue tighten. After a shave, the old barber in Adam's neighbourhood rubs a block of alum on his cheek, and the skin stings and pulls tight. Alum is an astringent. Years later, Adam's thesis draft comes back from his supervisor with sharp remarks on every page. Careless. Vague. Unsupported. The comments sting just like that alum, yet every one is fair. Astringent sounds like stringent, meaning strict, and both come from a Latin verb meaning to bind tight. So, what word describes criticism so sharp it stings? ... Astringent.

gre.s: The critic's ____ reviews, which spared neither famous names nor beginners, made her the most feared voice in the literary world.
gre.clue: spared neither famous names nor beginners

example: Her astringent comments on the committee's draft, though painful to hear, saved the project from several costly errors.

en: Self-evident; accepted as true without proof
hook: AXIOM: a basic truth in math, needing no proof.
story: Axiomatic. Self-evident; accepted as true without proof. Mandy's grandmother never studied economics, but she has run the family kitchen for fifty years on a few firm rules. Buy fish early, before the best ones are gone. Never trust a seller who will not let you touch the vegetables. To her, these truths are axiomatic. If you asked her for proof, she would only [chuckle] shake her head. An axiom is a basic truth in geometry, accepted without proof. So, what word describes a truth so obvious that no one needs to prove it? ... Axiomatic.

gre.s: It was once considered ____ that the sun revolved around the earth, a truth so plain that no one thought to question it, yet the assumption proved entirely false.
gre.clue: so plain that no one thought to question it

example: Among good cooks it is axiomatic that fresh ingredients matter more than any fancy technique.

en: To surrender or give in
hook: CAPITULATE: surrender your CAPITAL city.
story: Capitulate. To surrender or give in after resisting. For a whole week, a thin grey kitten cried outside the gate of Laila's house. Every evening Laila begged to keep it, and every evening her father said no. Then came a night of heavy rain. Her father opened the door, looked at the shivering kitten, [sigh] and carried it inside himself. After seven days of refusing, he had capitulated. Capitulate comes from the Latin for head, like capital, because terms of surrender were once written out under headings. So, what verb means to finally give in after holding out? ... Capitulate.

gre.s: After months of insisting that it would never negotiate, the management finally chose to ____ to the union's demands when the strike began to cripple production.
gre.clue: when the strike began to cripple production

example: After three hours of pleading from the twins, their mother capitulated and bought them ice cream before dinner.

en: To scold someone sharply for doing wrong
hook: CHASTISE: CHASE them with words until they're CHASTE (corrected).
story: Chastise. To scold someone sharply for doing wrong. Roy took his father's motorbike out at midnight without asking and came back with a dented mudguard. At breakfast, his father did not shout. He spoke slowly and sharply about trust, about danger, about Roy's mother lying awake. Roy stared at his paratha, his ears burning. He had never been chastised so thoroughly. Chastise comes from the same Latin root as chaste, meaning pure, as if a good scolding cleans out the fault. So, what verb means to scold someone sharply for a wrong? ... Chastise.

gre.s: Far from praising the minister's handling of the flood, the committee's report went out of its way to ____ him for delays that had cost lives.
gre.clue: Far from praising

example: The captain chastised her players for arriving late to training, reminding them that discipline wins tournaments.

en: Courteous, gallant, and honorable, especially toward women
hook: CHIVALROUS: like a medieval knight's CHIVALRY.
story: Chivalrous. Courteous, gallant and honourable, especially toward women. One rainy evening downtown, the street flooded knee-deep. An elderly woman and her granddaughter stood stranded at the edge, clutching their shopping bags. A young delivery rider parked his bicycle, carried their bags across, then came back and gave the old woman his arm, step by careful step. He would not take a single cent. It was a chivalrous act, and the people watching smiled. Chivalry was the code of medieval knights, and the word comes from the French for horseman. So, what word describes gallant, honourable courtesy? ... Chivalrous.

gre.s: In an age of cynicism, the soldier's ____ treatment of his captured enemies, whom he fed and sheltered, astonished his comrades.
gre.clue: whom he fed and sheltered

example: In a chivalrous gesture, the champion helped his fallen opponent to his feet before raising his own arms in victory.

en: To damage someone's reputation with false statements
hook: DE-FAME: destroy someone's FAME.
story: Defame. To damage someone's reputation with false statements. Keith ran a small sweet shop in town, known for its creamy yogurt. A rival began spreading a rumour that Keith mixed chalk into his yoghurt. It was a lie, but customers drifted away, and Keith sat alone behind his counter. When the rival was caught and fined, everyone saw how cruelly he had tried to defame an honest man. Hidden inside defame is fame, your good name; to defame someone is to tear that name down. So, what verb means to ruin a reputation with false claims? ... Defame.

gre.s: The politician's opponents sought to ____ him by spreading fabricated stories of corruption, hoping voters would believe the lies before they could be disproved.
gre.clue: spreading fabricated stories of corruption

example: The newspaper paid heavy damages after a court ruled that it had defamed a Sylhet surgeon with invented accusations.

en: Working well and producing the result that was wanted
hook: EFFICACIOUS: EFFECTIVE.
story: Efficacious. Working well and producing the result that was wanted. When little Zach caught a stomach bug one hot June, his grandmother did not panic. She mixed a packet of oral saline into clean water and fed it to him spoon by spoon. By evening he was sitting up, asking for biscuits. Researchers in South Asia helped prove, decades ago, how efficacious this simple drink is, and it has saved millions of children around the world. Efficacious is a formal cousin of effective; both come from the Latin for to accomplish. So, what word describes a remedy that truly works? ... Efficacious.

gre.s: The manufacturer touted the supplement as highly ____, yet independent trials showed that it relieved symptoms no better than a sugar pill.
gre.clue: relieved symptoms no better than a sugar pill

example: Across much of Africa, cheap insecticide-treated bed nets rank among the most efficacious tools public health workers have against malaria.

en: To decorate; to add details, often untrue, to make a story more interesting
hook: EMBELLISH: add BELLS to it, decorate.
story: Embellish. To decorate; also, to add details, often untrue, to make a story more exciting. Every winter, Seth's uncle tells the story of crossing the great river in a storm. First the waves were tall. The next year they were taller than the boat. By this winter, a crocodile was chasing them, and the children [laugh] shrieked. Uncle embellishes his tale the way Seth's mother embellishes a patchwork quilt, stitch by stitch. Hidden in embellish is the French belle, beautiful: to embellish is to make something prettier. So, what verb means to decorate a story with added details? ... Embellish.

gre.s: The journalist was dismissed when editors discovered her habit of choosing to ____ her reports with vivid quotations that no source had ever actually spoken.
gre.clue: vivid quotations that no source had ever actually spoken

example: The job candidate embellished his résumé, turning a two-week internship into a year of senior management experience.

en: Wide-ranging and thorough, covering almost every part of a subject
hook: ENCYCLOPEDIC: like an ENCYCLOPEDIA, knows everything.
story: Encyclopedic. Wide-ranging and thorough, covering almost every part of a subject. In the crowded lanes of the book market, an old bookseller named Reuben has a stall stacked to the ceiling. Ask him for a used chemistry guide or a rare poetry collection, and he climbs his ladder and pulls it out in a minute, dust and all. Piper once tested him with three forgotten titles. [gasp] He found all three. His knowledge of books is encyclopedic. Like an encyclopedia, an encyclopedic mind covers nearly everything in its field. So, what word describes knowledge that is broad and thorough? ... Encyclopedic.

gre.s: The guide's ____ knowledge of the city, extending from medieval architecture to the history of every street name, delighted the tourists.
gre.clue: extending from medieval architecture to the history of every street name

example: Professor Haque's encyclopedic grasp of Bengali folk music lets him name the district where almost any song began.

en: Making a wrong seem less serious; partially excusing
hook: EXTENUATING: makes the guilt more TENUOUS (thin).
story: Extenuating. Making a wrong seem less serious; partly excusing it. Shelby submitted her term paper two days late, and her department's rule was strict: late work gets zero. But on the due date, the river near her village had broken its embankment, and she had spent two days helping her family carry their belongings to higher ground. Her professor listened quietly, then accepted the paper. These were extenuating circumstances. Extenuating comes from the Latin for making thin, like tenuous: extenuating facts thin out the blame. So, what word describes circumstances that partly excuse a wrong? ... Extenuating.

gre.s: Although the judge acknowledged that the defendant had stolen the medicine, she cited ____ circumstances, noting that he had done so to save his dying child.
gre.clue: he had done so to save his dying child

example: The school accepted that a burst water pipe in the exam hall was an extenuating factor and allowed the students to resit.

en: Joking at the wrong moment about things that are serious
hook: FACETIOUS: makes funny FACES at serious things.
story: Facetious. Joking at the wrong moment about something serious. Spencer's family sat in the living room after his father's blood pressure report came back high. Everyone was worried. Spencer tried to lighten the mood. "Good news," he said, "now Dad has an excuse to skip the wedding feasts." Nobody laughed. His mother gave him a long, tired look. His facetious joke had fallen flat. A handy trick: facetious contains the vowels a, e, i, o, u in order. So, what word describes a joke made at the wrong time about something serious? ... Facetious.

gre.s: The minister's ____ remark about the flood victims, which he apparently intended as a joke, provoked outrage among families who had lost everything.
gre.clue: which he apparently intended as a joke

example: Asked how the company would repay its debts, the chief executive gave a facetious reply about winning the lottery.

en: Not perfect, and so sometimes wrong or mistaken
hook: FALLIBLE: able to FALL into error.
story: Fallible. Not perfect, and so sometimes wrong or mistaken. Mason's cricket coach was a local legend, and the boys trusted his every word. One season he moved Mason down the batting order, and Mason's scores fell. After a month, the coach called him aside. "I was wrong. Go back to opening." Mason was stunned, but he respected the coach more than ever. Even the best coaches are fallible, and the wise ones admit it. Fallible shares its root with false and fail; its opposite, infallible, means never wrong. So, what word describes anyone capable of making mistakes? ... Fallible.

gre.s: Eyewitness testimony, once treated as nearly conclusive, is now known to be highly ____, since memories can be distorted by stress, suggestion, and the passage of time.
gre.clue: memories can be distorted by stress, suggestion, and the passage of time

example: Even the most advanced weather models are fallible, so farmers in Rangpur still watch the sky before sowing.

en: A deceptive movement meant to distract an opponent
hook: FEINT: a FAKE move. Sounds like FAINT but means FAKE.
story: Feint. A deceptive movement meant to distract an opponent. In a village kabaddi match, Tanner crossed into the other team's half, chanting under his breath. He lunged left as if to touch the nearest defender. Three defenders shifted left to trap him. In that instant he spun right, tagged the last player, and dashed home. The crowd roared. His lunge had been a feint. Feint sounds exactly like faint, but think of a fake: a feint is a fake move, made to fool. So, what word names a fake move that tricks an opponent? ... Feint.

gre.s: The general's apparent retreat was merely a ____: while the enemy rushed to pursue, his main force circled behind them and attacked their unguarded camp.
gre.clue: while the enemy rushed to pursue, his main force circled behind them

example: The chess master's queen move looked like an attack but was only a feint to pull the defending pieces out of position.

en: Socially awkward; lacking grace or tact
hook: GAUCHE: French for LEFT, as in left-handed and clumsy.
story: Gauche. Socially awkward; lacking grace or tact. The first time Frank met his fiancée's family in the old city, he wanted so badly to impress them. Instead, he knocked over a glass of spiced yogurt drink, called her grandmother by the wrong name, and asked her uncle how much his house had cost. Everyone smiled politely. Later, in the rickshaw, Frank [sigh] groaned at how gauche he had been. Gauche is French for left, from an old belief that the left hand is clumsy; its opposite, adroit, comes from the French for right. So, what word describes someone socially clumsy and tactless? ... Gauche.

gre.s: Though brilliant in the laboratory, the young chemist was painfully ____ at receptions, blurting out tactless remarks and forgetting the names of her hosts.
gre.clue: blurting out tactless remarks

example: As a gauche teenager, I once congratulated a guest on her pregnancy when she was simply wearing a loose dress.

en: Looking or feeling sad and gloomy
hook: GLUM: GLOOMY + DUMB-struck.
story: Glum. Looking or feeling sad and gloomy. Rain had been falling on the port city for three days, and the school picnic to the beach was cancelled. Little Sadie sat by the window with her chin in her hands. She would not eat her lunch, and she would not talk. Her father sat beside her quietly for a while, then gently asked, "Why so glum?" Glum sounds like a short, heavy cousin of gloom, and it means the same heavy mood. So, what word describes a face that is sad and gloomy? ... Glum.

gre.s: Despite the company's record profits, the shareholders' meeting was strangely ____, since everyone knew the beloved founder would announce his resignation.
gre.clue: since everyone knew the beloved founder would announce his resignation

example: The glum faces of the waiting passengers told me that the flight to Cox's Bazar had been delayed yet again.

en: Rude and disrespectful; not showing proper respect
hook: IM-PERTINENT: not pertinent (relevant), and rude to boot.
story: Impertinent. Rude and disrespectful; not showing proper respect. At a family dinner, Nora's teenage cousin was asked by their grandfather about his exam results. The boy did not even look up from his phone. "You would not understand my results anyway." The table fell silent. His mother's face went red, and the grandfather slowly set down his glass. It was an impertinent answer. Impertinent literally means not pertinent: an impertinent remark has no place in the conversation, and it is rude besides. So, what word describes a cheeky, disrespectful reply to an elder? ... Impertinent.

gre.s: The young reporter's ____ questions about the senator's private life drew a sharp rebuke from the press secretary.
gre.clue: drew a sharp rebuke

example: The impertinent customer told the elderly tailor that he was far too old to understand modern fashion.

en: Never tiring; persistently energetic
hook: IN-DE-FATIGABLE: cannot be FATIGUED.
story: Indefatigable. Never tiring; persistently energetic. In a southern fishing village, a retired teacher named Rose runs free evening classes for children. After teaching, she visits families who keep their girls at home, walks miles along sandy paths, and returns the next day to try again. Volunteers half her age struggle to keep up. "Where does she get the energy?" they whisper. She is indefatigable. Break it apart: in means not, and fatigable means able to be fatigued, so an indefatigable person can never be worn out. So, what word describes someone who never tires? ... Indefatigable.

gre.s: Even in her nineties, the ____ activist continued to march at every protest, outlasting colleagues half her age.
gre.clue: outlasting colleagues half her age

example: The indefatigable archivist spent twelve years cataloguing every letter in the old zamindar family's collection.

en: Impossible to understand or interpret
hook: IN-SCRUTABLE: can't be SCRUTINIZED.
story: Inscrutable. Impossible to understand or interpret. Every Friday, Tessa's grandfather plays chess with his oldest friend under the banyan tree near the church. Tessa watches the friend's face for clues, but it never changes: no smile, no frown, not even a blink before a winning move. Is he worried? Is he about to win? Nobody can tell. Grandfather calls him the sphinx. His face is truly inscrutable. Scrutiny means close examination, so something inscrutable stays a mystery no matter how closely you examine it. So, what word describes a face that no one can read? ... Inscrutable.

gre.s: The cat's ____ expression gave no hint of whether it was about to purr contentedly or lash out with its claws.
gre.clue: gave no hint

example: The ancient Indus script remains inscrutable, since no one has yet found a bilingual inscription that would help decode it.

en: To throw away or abandon something unwanted
hook: JETTISON: a JET dumping fuel to lighten its load.
story: Jettison. To throw away or abandon something unwanted. Halfway across a wide river, a small trawler began to take on water in the rising waves. The boatman shouted, and the passengers worked fast, heaving sacks of potatoes and empty drums over the side. The boat rode higher, and everyone reached the bank safely. [sigh] They had jettisoned the cargo to save themselves. In the same way, a company can jettison a failing plan. Picture a jet dumping fuel to lighten its load before an emergency landing. So, what verb means to throw away what you no longer want? ... Jettison.

gre.s: Faced with mounting losses, the company decided to ____ its least profitable divisions so that it could focus its resources on its core business.
gre.clue: so that it could focus its resources on its core business

example: The design team jettisoned their original logo after customers said it looked like a broken umbrella.

en: Lacking energy; relaxed and slow
hook: LANGUID: LANGUISHING, lazy.
story: Languid. Lacking energy; relaxed and slow. It is a hot Friday afternoon in May. After a heavy lunch of rice and fish curry, Ian's whole family lies on the cool floor under the ceiling fan. Nobody talks. The cat stretches, yawns, and closes its eyes. Even the street outside is quiet, except for one far-off crow. Ian thinks he has never felt so languid. Languid and languish share a Latin root meaning to be faint or weak, and a languid afternoon moves at half speed. So, what word describes a slow, lazy, low-energy mood? ... Languid.

gre.s: The afternoon heat made everyone ____: even the usually restless children lay on the cool floor, too sluggish to play or even talk.
gre.clue: too sluggish to play or even talk

example: The cat stretched languidly across the warm windowsill, ignoring the pigeons that strutted just outside the glass.

en: To lose strength; to suffer from being in an unpleasant situation
bn: দুর্বল হয়ে পড়া; কষ্টে দিন কাটানো
hook: LANGUISH: become LANGUID, weak and fading.
story: Languish. To lose strength; to suffer from being in an unpleasant situation. When Tina's family moved to a small city flat, her grandmother's basil plant came too. On a dark balcony with no sun, it began to languish, its leaves pale and drooping. Her grandmother was languishing too; she missed her village courtyard. One weekend, Tina carried the plant up to the rooftop, and took her grandmother up with it. Both seemed to come alive again. Languish shares its root with languid. So, what verb means to grow weak while stuck in a bad situation? ... Languish.

gre.s: Without fresh investment, the once thriving port continued to ____, its warehouses empty and its docks slowly crumbling into the harbor.
gre.clue: its warehouses empty and its docks slowly crumbling

example: Plans for the new metro line languished in government files for twenty years before construction finally began.

en: A person who freely indulges in pleasures, ignoring moral restraints
hook: LIBERTINE: takes too many LIBERTIES with morality.
story: Libertine. A person who freely indulges in pleasures, ignoring moral restraints. In an old novel that Nadia reads for her literature class, a landlord's son wastes his father's fortune on card games, wine and parties that last until dawn. He laughs at every warning, breaks every promise, and answers to no one. His mother watches the estate slowly crumble. In the margin, Nadia writes one word: libertine. Libertine shares a root with liberty, but a libertine takes liberty too far, with no self-control at all. So, what do you call a person who chases pleasure and ignores morals? ... Libertine.

gre.s: Unlike his brother, a notorious ____ who squandered his fortune on drink and gambling, the younger prince lived a life of strict self-discipline.
gre.clue: squandered his fortune on drink and gambling

example: Lord Byron was known in London society as a libertine whose love affairs and debts fed endless gossip.

en: An artistic work imitating the style of other works; a medley
hook: PASTICHE: a PASTE of different styles glued together.
story: Pastiche. An artistic work that imitates the styles of other works; a medley. At a university cultural night, Sam's band played one song that began like an old folk tune, slid into a classic ballad, and ended with a roaring rock guitar solo. The audience [laugh] cheered and clapped along. A music teacher in the front row smiled and called it a clever pastiche. Pastiche comes from the Italian pasticcio, a pie that mixes many ingredients, so picture a pie baked from borrowed styles. So, what word names a work stitched together by imitating other styles? ... Pastiche.

gre.s: Critics dismissed the film as a mere ____, cobbled together from scenes borrowed from a dozen earlier thrillers and lacking any style of its own.
gre.clue: cobbled together from scenes borrowed from a dozen earlier thrillers

example: The new shopping mall is an odd pastiche of Greek columns, Mughal domes and mirrored glass towers.

en: A particular fondness for something over other things
hook: PRE-DILECTION: PRE-selected as your DELIGHT.
story: Predilection. A particular fondness for something over other things. Every evening, when the snack seller rings his bell, Tessa runs downstairs. She has tried every new café in the area, but nothing beats spicy street snacks with extra tamarind water and a pinch of green chilli. Her friends tease her, but she just [laugh] orders another plate. Her predilection for street snacks is famous in the family. Predilection comes from Latin roots meaning to choose before others: a predilection is the thing you pick first, every time. So, what word means a special fondness for one thing over others? ... Predilection.

gre.s: The collector's ____ for small Dutch landscapes was well known, and dealers saved such paintings especially for him.
gre.clue: dealers saved such paintings especially for him

example: The physicist had a predilection for old detective novels, which she read on every long flight to conferences.

en: To finally agree after refusing; to become less severe
hook: RELENT: finally LET it go.
story: Relent. To finally agree after refusing; also, to become less severe. For a week, Jody begged to join her university trip to the hills, and every day her mother said no. Then on Thursday evening, the heavy rain that had drummed on their roof all week finally relented, and so did her mother. "Go," she said, "but call me every night." Jody [laugh] hugged her so hard they both nearly fell over. Do not confuse relent with relentless, which means never easing up; to relent is the opposite, to soften. So, what verb means to give in after refusing? ... Relent.

gre.s: The authorities refused for months to release the detained journalist, but mounting international pressure eventually forced them to ____.
gre.clue: refused for months

example: The heavy rain finally relented around noon, and the groundsmen hurried to pull the covers off the pitch.

en: Curving and bending, often in a smooth, graceful way
hook: SINUOUS: like a SNAKE's S-curves.
story: Sinuous. Curving and bending, often in a smooth, graceful way. On her first flight south over the delta, Annie pressed her face to the window. Below, the rivers wound across the green land in great silver loops, bending back on themselves like ribbons. [gasp] She had never seen anything so beautiful. At a dance recital later, she noticed the same sinuous grace in a dancer's arms. Sinuous comes from the Latin sinus, a curve or fold; do not confuse it with sinewy, which means tough and muscular. So, what word describes a river that winds in smooth curves? ... Sinuous.

gre.s: Unlike the straight highways of the plains, the mountain road was ____, twisting back on itself so many times that several passengers grew carsick.
gre.clue: twisting back on itself so many times

example: The dancer's sinuous arm movements made the old Manipuri dance look as smooth as flowing water.

en: To take someone's place, often by plotting or force
hook: SUP-PLANT: uproot one PLANT and put another in its place.
story: Supplant. To take someone's place, often by plotting or force. Nadia's grandmother often tells a story from her father's old office in a river port town. A charming young clerk joined, helpful to everyone. But behind the manager's back, he whispered to the owner, took credit for others' work, and slowly won the owner's trust. Within a year, he had supplanted the loyal old manager entirely. The Latin root means to trip someone up by the sole of the foot, and that is exactly how a schemer supplants a rival. So, what verb means to push someone out and take their place? ... Supplant.

gre.s: The ambitious deputy spent years flattering the board and quietly undermining his superior, plotting all the while to ____ her as head of the company.
gre.clue: quietly undermining his superior

example: The young striker gradually supplanted the veteran captain in the starting eleven, scoring in nine straight matches.

en: Empty of real ideas or intelligence; blank
hook: VACUOUS: like a VACUUM, empty inside.
story: Vacuous. Empty of real ideas or intelligence; blank. On a television talk show, a young politician was asked how he would fix the city's traffic. He smiled widely. "Traffic is a big problem, and we will solve it with solutions. The future is very bright." Then he said nothing more. Fiona, watching at home, turned to her father in disbelief. He [chuckle] shook his head. "What a vacuous answer." Vacuous shares its root with vacuum and vacant: nothing inside. So, what word describes an answer, or a stare, that is empty of thought? ... Vacuous.

gre.s: The candidate's speeches, full of rousing slogans but devoid of any concrete policy proposals, struck most serious analysts as ____.
gre.clue: devoid of any concrete policy proposals

example: The quiz contestant gave a vacuous grin when asked to name the capital of Australia.

en: Offering nothing stimulating or challenging; dull and empty
hook: VAPID: like VAPOR, empty air.
story: Vapid. Offering nothing stimulating or challenging; dull and empty. Matt's cousin forwarded him a famous motivational video. Twenty minutes of slow piano music and lines like "Believe in yourself" and "Dreams come true." Not one useful idea. Matt yawned and closed it halfway. Later, his cousin asked what he thought. Matt searched for a polite word, but the only honest one was vapid. Vapid comes from the Latin for flat, the way wine tastes when it has lost its flavour. A vapid talk is flat. So, what word describes talk that is flat, dull and empty? ... Vapid.

gre.s: The critic dismissed the pop song's lyrics as ____, a string of empty phrases that said nothing at all about love.
gre.clue: a string of empty phrases that said nothing at all

example: The award show's vapid speeches, all thanks and no ideas, sent half the audience back to their phones.
